methods.label: Compare with the radial point
methods.explanation:
The useful comparison point is where the ray from the center through \(A\) meets the circle. We will show that this point is nearest to \(A\).

Write \(r=PB>0\). First, if \(A=P\), every point on the circle is distance \(r\) from \(A\), so \(P\) belongs to the required set.

Now suppose \(A\ne P\). Let \(t=PA>0\), and let \(Q\) be the point where ray \(PA\) meets the circle. Since \(A\) and \(Q\) lie on the same ray,
\[
AQ=|t-r|.
\]
This covers points \(A\) inside, on, and outside the circle. For any point \(X\) on the circle, the triangle inequality gives
\[
t\le AX+r,\qquad r\le AX+t.
\]
Together these imply \(AX\ge |t-r|=AQ\).

If \(P,A,X\) are not collinear, both triangle inequalities are strict, so \(AX>AQ\). If they are collinear, \(X\) is either \(Q\) or the opposite point on the circle. That opposite point is distance \(t+r>|t-r|\) from \(A\), since \(t,r>0\). Thus \(Q\) is the unique nearest circle point when \(A\ne P\).

Consequently, \(B\) is nearest exactly when \(Q=B\), which means that \(A\) lies on ray \(PB\). Including the center case, the answer is the ray beginning at \(P\) and passing through \(B\), choice B.
